sections.title: OCaml and Java Concepts; Tail Recursion

items.prompt: True or false: (a) In Java, an array's length cannot change once it is allocated. (b) In both Java and OCaml, == tests whether two values have the same structure. (c) As in Java, an OCaml identifier can have the value null. (d) In OCaml (as taught in CIS 1200), a record of closures is the closest analog to a Java object.
items.key: (a) True; (b) False; (c) False; (d) True
items.notes: The PDF has four statements, (a) to (d). == is reference equality in Java and physical equality in OCaml; OCaml has no null (use options).

items.prompt: Is this mystery function tail recursive?
items.code:
let rec mystery (ls : int list) : unit =
  begin match ls with
  | [] -> ()
  | hd :: tl -> print_int hd; mystery tl
  end
items.key: Tail recursive

items.prompt: Is this mystery function tail recursive?
items.code:
let rec mystery (ls : int list) : int =
  begin match ls with
  | [] -> 0
  | [x] -> x
  | x :: y :: tl -> mystery ((y - x) :: tl)
  end
items.key: Tail recursive

items.prompt: Is this mystery function tail recursive?
items.code:
let rec mystery (ls : (int -> int) list) (x : int) : int =
  begin match ls with
  | [] -> x
  | f :: tl -> f (mystery tl x)
  end
items.key: Not tail recursive
items.notes: The result of the recursive call is passed to f, so work remains after the call.

items.prompt: Is this mystery function tail recursive?
items.key: Not tail recursive
items.notes: The call mystery (x - 1) in the if-condition is not in tail position, even though the two branch calls are.

items.prompt: The picture shows q with head pointing to node {v=1} and tail pointing to node {v=3}; node 1's next points to node 3, and node 3's next is None. Draw the heap after mystery 1 q runs (ignore temporary stack bindings).
items.key: q.head -> node {v=1}; node1.next -> NEW node {v=2}; node2.next -> node {v=3}; node3.next = None; q.tail -> node3. (Node 1 equals elt, so it is skipped. Node 3 is not elt, so a new node with v = 3 - 1 = 2 is linked in front of it through node1.next.)

items.prompt: For the call mystery 1 q above, are the queue invariants preserved? (Yes/No)
items.key: Yes

items.prompt: Does mystery always preserve the queue invariants? If yes, explain why. If no, give a valid q and an elt that break the queue, and name the violated invariant (1, 2a, or 2b).
items.key: Yes, always: each non-elt node gets a new node linked in front of it, the tail stays last with next = None, and the "insert before head" case just reassigns head.
items.notes: The answer (always preserved) is correct, but part of the explanation is not accurate. When the head node is not elt (qnpo = None), the code does q.head <- qno, and qno is the head node itself, not Some node. So head is set to the value it already has, and the new node is never linked in; it is just garbage. A non-elt head node therefore does NOT get a new node in front of it. A more accurate reason: the code only ever writes q.head (to its current value) or prev.next <- Some node where node.next points to the original next node. So the chain from head still reaches the unchanged tail (2a), tail.next is never written and stays None (2b), and an empty queue is left alone (1). Also, qn.v - 1 forces 'a = int, so mystery works only on int queues despite the 'a annotation.

items.prompt: Write count_exact q pred count, which returns true if exactly count node values in a valid queue satisfy pred, and false otherwise. For full credit it must be tail recursive and exit early (traverse the whole queue only when needed). Tests: for the queue 1,2,3 with an is-even predicate, count 1 gives true and count 2 gives false.
items.notes: The recursive calls are tail calls because the right operand of && is in tail position in OCaml. The function exits early as soon as seen > count.

sections.title: OCaml ASM, Mutable State, and Closures

items.prompt: The picture shows a stack with z and w. z points to a heap cell Cons(1, Nil). w points to a heap cell Cons(2, •), and its tail pointer goes to that same Cons(1, Nil) cell. There are only two heap cells and no other stack bindings. Does this program build exactly that ASM state?
items.code:
let z = Cons(1, Nil)
let w = Cons(2, Cons(1, Nil))
items.key: Does not build it (w's tail is a second, separate Cons(1, Nil) cell, so z and w do not share)

items.key:
let mousedrag_listener (action_if_drag : Gctx.position -> unit)
                       (action_otherwise : unit -> unit) : event_listener =
  fun (g : Gctx.gctx) (e : Gctx.event) ->
    let p = Gctx.event_pos e g in
    begin match Gctx.event_type e with
    | MouseDrag -> action_if_drag p
    | _ -> action_otherwise ()
    end
items.notes: Only the match arms are blank. The exam skeleton writes event_pos and event_type without the Gctx. prefix, while the key adds it. Either form is fine as long as the module is in scope; if Gctx is not opened, the constructor would need to be written Gctx.MouseDrag.

items.prompt: Implement reshape(input, m, n), which fills an m x n int array row by row from input. Every row except the last must be full. The last row must hold at least one input element and is padded with 0. Return null if this is impossible. Example: {5,2,8,1,3,4,7,6} with m = n = 3 gives rows [5,2,8], [1,3,4], [7,6,0]. Assume input is non-null and m, n >= 0.
items.notes: The null check encodes (m-1)*n < input.length <= m*n, which matches the spec in normal cases. Edge cases the spec leaves open: (1) n = 0 always gives null. (2) m >= 1 with an empty input gives null, since the last row cannot contain an element. (3) m = 0, n > 0 and an empty input gives new int[0][n] rather than null; there is no 'last row', so the rule is arguably satisfied vacuously, but m = 0, n = 0 and an empty input gives null. These are inconsistent but unlikely to be graded. The PDF numbers this question only '5', with no sub-items.
